phonemes.desc: Voiceless aspirated velar [kʰ] — pinyin k, said with a visible puff of breath.
Close back vowel [ʊ] plus velar nasal [ŋ], on the dipping third tone: the pitch falls, then rises.
Voiceless unaspirated alveolar [ts] — pinyin z, closer to English “ds” than “z.”
The apical vowel [ɨ], a tongue-tip vowel with no English equivalent, also on the third tone; in the flowing phrase, sandhi lifts the first syllable to second tone: Kóngzǐ.

pronunciation.approximation: “KOHNG-dzuh,” each syllable on a dipping-then-rising melody; said in one breath, the first tone lifts and the second dips.

kin.label: Chinese honorific
kin.form: 孔夫子 Kǒng Fūzǐ, “Master Kong” — the fuller honorific from which the Jesuits of Matteo Ricci’s circle coined the Latin name Confucius (late 16th c.).

kin.label: Courtesy name
kin.form: 仲尼 Zhòngní, the Master’s courtesy name (zì 字), the form early texts prefer for addressing him.

kin.label: Surname
kin.form: 孔 Kǒng, the family name — the stock from which the Kong lineage of Qufu still descends.

pronunciation.note: Kǒngzǐ is Tier 1 because both syllables carry the third tone, marked by the carons ǒ and ǐ — tone is a lexical feature of Mandarin that the plain ASCII “kongzi” erases entirely. (The older entry described “stress and length”; the operative features are the two tone marks.)

domains.title: Confucius
domains.subtitle: Confucius, Moral Teaching, Ritual
domains.lead: Kǒngzǐ — Master Kong, Latinized by Jesuits as Confucius — is the teacher of China: the man who made learning, ritual propriety (lǐ 禮), and humaneness (rén 仁) the foundation of the good life and the good state. He claimed no revelation and no divinity — only transmission of the ancients — and became, for two and a half millennia, the archetype of the teacher.

cards.name: Rén — Humaneness
cards.desc: The core of his ethics: the fellow-feeling that makes one truly human; “loving others” is its shortest definition (Analects 12.22).

cards.name: Lǐ — Ritual Propriety
cards.desc: The rites that choreograph every relationship, from ancestral sacrifice to the cup offered a guest: reverence made visible.

cards.name: Tiān — Heaven
cards.desc: He spoke rarely of spirits but constantly of Heaven’s mandate (tiānmìng) as the moral horizon of conduct (Analects 3.13).

cards.name: The Analects
cards.desc: The Lúnyǔ 論語, “selected sayings,” compiled by disciples after his death — the core text of East Asian education for two thousand years.

symbols.name: Qilin of the birth-omen
symbols.meaning: The peace-beast said to have appeared before his birth, spitting a jade tablet announcing a child whose teaching would rule all under Heaven though he sat on no throne (later legend built on Shiji 47).

symbols.name: The Apricot Altar (Xíngtán 杏壇)
symbols.meaning: The teaching ground at Qufu where tradition seats the Master among his disciples; the phrase became a synonym for the school itself.

symbols.name: The Analects (Lúnyǔ 論語)
symbols.meaning: Twenty books of short exchanges — question, answer, sometimes only a sigh: the irreducible core of the tradition, memorized by every educated East Asian for two millennia.

symbols.name: The Stone Classics
symbols.meaning: The canon carved into stone at the imperial academy (the Xīpíng stones, 175–183 CE) so that no scribal error could corrupt the Master’s text.

symbols.name: The cypress of Qufu
symbols.meaning: The ancient cypresses at his tomb in the Kong Lin forest cemetery — living links in the longest documented family line on earth.

mythology.lead: Kǒngzǐ is a historical man — born 551 BCE in the state of Lǔ — but the tradition did with his biography what it does with all founders: it polished it into legend. The Shǐjì of Sīmǎ Qiān (ch. 47) supplies the framework, the Lúnyǔ the voice; between them stands the mythic Master, born under a portent, refused by every court, and vindicated only after death.

myths.title: The Qilin’s Jade Tablet (551 BCE)
myths.text: The legends of the Master’s birth are later embroidery on a plain record — Sīmǎ Qiān’s Shiji 47 says only that Kǒng Qiū was born in 551 BCE at Zōu in Lǔ, posthumous son of the aged soldier Kǒng Shūliáng Hé and the young Yán Zhēngzài. But tradition could not leave a founder without a portent: a qilin, the unicorn-beast that appears only when a sage is to come, was said to have entered the family courtyard and spat a jade tablet announcing a son whose doctrine would rule all under Heaven, though he would sit on no throne. The tablet bore the character for “hill” (qiū), and the child received it as his personal name — matching Mount Ni, beside which he was born — and the courtesy name Zhòngní, “second-born Ni.” Han thinkers gave the idea its name: the Master was the sùwáng, the “uncrowned king,” whose kingdom was the text. The legend means the tradition knew exactly what it had.

myths.title: The Master Asks Lǎozǐ About Rites
myths.text: In his thirties the young Kǒngzǐ travelled west to the royal capital of Zhōu to question the aged archivist Lǎozǐ about the rites of burial and mourning. Lǎozǐ, tradition says, received him coolly: “The men of whom you speak are bones now, and their words died with them… I have heard that a good merchant hides his store as though it were empty, and that a noble man in his bearing looks like a fool. Cast off your pride and your many desires — for neither profits you. That is all I have to say to you.” The Master returned and told his disciples: “I know how birds fly, how fish swim, how beasts run — but the dragon I cannot fathom, riding the wind and clouds up into Heaven. Today I have seen Lǎozǐ: he is such a dragon.” (Shiji 63.) The meeting is the tradition’s way of contrasting its two great teachers — the one who withdrew, and the one who knocked on every door.

myths.title: Fourteen Years Between the States
myths.text: From 497 to 484 BCE the Master wandered — Wèi, Chén, Cài, Chǔ — offering his Way to rulers who would not buy it. The Analects keeps the human record. At the border pass of Yì, the warden, watching a whole generation of pupils following one unheeded man, sought him out: “Heaven is going to use the Master as a wooden bell” — the clapper that warns a sleeping age (3.24). In Chǔ the madman Jiēyú passed his carriage singing: “Phoenix, phoenix, how your virtue has declined!… The past is beyond mending, but the future can still be pursued. Give it up, give it up — those who serve in court now court death” (18.5). The Master climbed down wanting to speak with him, but Jiēyú fled. Between Chén and Cài the party was cornered and out of food; the Shiji adds the scene the disciples themselves laughed at — cornered and helpless, the Master said they were “like stray dogs,” and smiled: “Yes, yes — stray dogs indeed.” The road means what he told the recluses: “If the Way prevailed in the world, I would not need to change anything” (18.6). And still he walked.

myths.title: “I Transmit, I Do Not Create”
myths.text: At sixty-eight the Master was called home to Lǔ, and his last five years were his real victory — not in office but in editing: he arranged the Odes and the Documents, said the tradition, and wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals so that “rebellious ministers and villainous sons would be struck with terror.” “I transmit but do not create,” he said; “I trust and love antiquity” (Analects 7.1). The book keeps the cost. When his best pupil, Yán Huí, died young, the Master wept without restraint: “Heaven has bereft me! Heaven has bereft me!” (11.9). In 479 BCE he died; the Shiji has him dream of a sacrificial tripod by his door and sing, days before: “The great mountain must crumble, the stout beam must break, the wise man must wither away.” The lament means the tradition understood: a teacher’s immortality is entirely in the students — and Yán Huí’s death is the wound the Analects never closes.

lore.syncretism: The Master resisted deification in life — “while you do not yet know life, how can you know death?” (Analects 11.12) — but the Han state deified him anyway. Emperor Gāozǔ offered the first imperial sacrifice at his tomb in 195 BCE; by the Tang his posthumous titles swelled toward “King” and “Perfect Sage,” and Dǒng Zhòngshū gave his teaching cosmological armor. From Sòng times the neo-Confucians — above all Zhū Xī — rebuilt it into the metaphysics of East Asia, and for thirteen centuries the civil examinations made his classics the gateway to office in China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. The West received him through the Jesuits: Ricci’s circle Latinized Kǒng Fūzǐ as Confucius, and Voltaire kept his portrait like a household saint. Modernity first dethroned him — the New Culture Movement denounced him as the face of feudalism — and then reinstated him. Few mortals have been so many things to so many regimes.
lore.culturalLegacy: His living monument is Qufu: the Temple of Confucius — consecrated in 478 BCE, the year after his death, when Duke Āi of Lǔ turned his former residence into a shrine — the adjacent Kong Mansion, and the Kong Lin cemetery, together the largest classical building complex in China after the Forbidden City. His bloodline is on record longer than any other on earth: the Kong genealogy counts more than eighty documented generations. From 605 to 1905 the empire’s examinations were built on his classics, making him — by crib-book, temple sacrifice, and schoolhouse portrait — the single most studied author in human history. Taiwan still keeps Teachers’ Day on his traditional birthday, 28 September; and the everyday word rú 儒, “scholar,” is his school’s oldest name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Kǒngzǐ is the rare founder who disclaimed founding anything. “I transmit, I do not create.” What he transmitted was a question rather than an answer: how should a human being live among other human beings? His answers were deliberately unheroic — learn, practice the rites, keep your word, honor your parents, govern by example — and the unheroism is their strength. He is the teacher as such, the man whose greatness is measured entirely in students.

The restoration of his name matters in a way he might have appreciated: drop a single tone-mark and the Master’s name dissolves into a string of letters. Orthography, he taught by every example of his life, is not decoration but the foundation of the Way. To write Kǒngzǐ is to keep the bell ringing.

lore.archaeology: Qufu is the material anchor: the Temple of Confucius stands on the site of his residence, consecrated by Duke Āi of Lǔ in 478 BCE and rebuilt to its present Ming-era scale; beside it the Kong Mansion housed his descendants until 1949, and the Kong Lin cemetery holds over 100,000 lineage burials with thousands of stelae. Far older than any temple, the Guōdiàn bamboo slips — a Warring States library buried c. 300 BCE at Hubei and excavated in 1993 — preserve pre-imperial versions of texts in his tradition, proving the school was copying and teaching his books within three centuries of his death. And the Wǔ Liáng shrine stone reliefs (Shandong, 151 CE) already show the iconic scene of the young Kǒngzǐ asking Lǎozǐ about the rites: the myth cut in stone within three and a half centuries of the man.
